facts.claim: Queen Victoria's wedding dress (RCIN 71975) is attributed to Mary Bettans, a court dressmaker, and was worn for her marriage to Prince Albert on 10 February 1840. Royal Collection Trust says the dress was notable for establishing a form of bridal fashion that persists today, 'formalising as it did the wearing of white wedding dresses', and that her choice made white desirable at all levels of society and a symbol of romantic love and purity.
facts.replaces: fact_12 (date, collection number and role in popularising white; read in full via Apify, rendered text)

facts.claim: Britannica (Today in History, 10 February): Victoria wore a white satin gown with British-made lace, a wreath of orange blossoms and an 18-foot train; she chose white because she liked the simple style and wanted to support the struggling British lace industry, not for the meanings of purity and wealth attached to it later. Twelve bridesmaids also wore white. Her wedding was widely publicised, unlike earlier low-key royal weddings in state robes.
facts.conflicts: The page headline says 'The Bride Wore White (for the First Time)', but Britannica's own 'Why Do Brides Wear White?' (fact_302) and the brief say white was not new, only rare. Do not repeat 'first time'; write 'popularised'. RCT (fact_300) says the dress has a Honiton lace flounce per batch A; Britannica 'Why Do Brides Wear White?' names Honiton lace, so 'Honiton lace' is now sourced (fact_302).

facts.claim: Britannica ('Why Do Brides Wear White?'): for many centuries in Western societies wedding dresses were of all different colours; brides tended to buy a dress they could wear again or simply wore the best dress they already owned, and white was impractical to keep clean. Today's white dress is largely thanks to a trend that began with Queen Victoria's 1840 wedding; she reportedly chose white to show off Honiton lace from the struggling British lace industry. The trend was first taken up by wealthier brides, spread across all economic levels, and was cemented as 'tradition' in the 20th century.
facts.replaces: [[VERIFY: what brides wore before 1840]] (resolved at encyclopaedia level; no V&A page found) and supports fact_12

facts.claim: MYTH, now sourced as such: Britannica says 'a few sources suggest' ancient cultures put the ring on the fourth finger of the left hand because they believed the 'vena amoris' or 'vein of love' ran from there directly to the heart, and that modern medicine has shown there is no such vein. (Britannica does not name Henry Swinburne or a date.)
facts.replaces: fact_13 (myth status and 'no such vein'; Wikipedia no longer needed for these points). The Swinburne 1686 attribution remains unsourced.

facts.claim: Britannica (Alicja Zelazko, fact-checked by Britannica Editors): the custom of giving a bride-to-be a ring may have started with the ancient Egyptians, but the earliest concrete evidence of engagement rings is Roman. Romans treated the ring as a sign of a legal agreement to marry; a woman traditionally received an iron ring, and women from wealthier families also received a gold ring worn in public. In the 12th century the Roman Catholic Church made marriage a sacrament and brought placing a ring on the bride's finger into the ceremony.

Britannica: in some South American countries such as Chile and Brazil, each partner wears a ring on the fourth finger of the right hand during the engagement and moves it to the fourth finger of the left hand at the wedding.
facts.replaces: [[VERIFY: which countries wear the ring on the right hand]] (partly: Chile and Brazil engagement only; other right-hand countries still unsourced)

insider_details.detail: When couples ask whether the white dress is 'traditional', the honest answer is that it is a Victorian fashion that became tradition: before 1840 brides wore their best dress in any colour, so a coloured or re-wearable dress for a destination wedding has strong historical precedent.

For couples marrying in Chile or Brazil, or with family from there, expect rings worn on the right hand during the engagement and moved to the left at the ceremony; plan a moment in the order of service for the switch.
The 'vein of love' line makes a lovely celebrant moment, but it should be framed as a story people once believed, not anatomy: Britannica is clear no such vein exists.
